content: The communication skills of doctors during labor and childbirth were evaluated two weeks postpartum using a modified version of the WHO Recommendations for Intrapartum Care for a Positive Childbirth Experience (MISS-21). In a study conducted in the United Kingdom, 140 midwives and doctors were randomized into one of four obstetric emergency training interventions: a one-day course at a local hospital, a one-day course at a simulation center, a two-day course with teamwork training at a local hospital, or a two-day course with teamwork training at a simulation center. The training included lectures, video demonstrations, and activities to highlight teamwork components. Before and after the training, participants managed three standardized simulated obstetric emergencies (eclampsia, postpartum hemorrhage, and shoulder dystocia) in a delivery room at their hospital. Outcomes were assessed based on the quality of care in communication, safety, and respect during these simulated emergencies three weeks post-training. Patient-actors, who were experienced midwives blinded to group allocation, provided feedback using a five-point Likert scale to evaluate statements such as, I felt well-informed due to good communication. A comparison of effective communication by healthcare staff versus usual practice revealed mixed results. A study from Syria found little to no difference in women's satisfaction scores, with very low-certainty evidence. Observational checklist scores assessing clinicians' communicative behavior before and after the intervention also showed minimal differences. Similarly, a UK study found very low-certainty evidence of improved patient-actor perceptions of care following clinician training for managing obstetric emergencies. Training conducted at local hospitals appeared to improve perceptions of safety and communication compared to training at simulation centers. However, for scenarios like eclampsia and shoulder dystocia, there was little to no improvement in patient-actor perceptions of communication. The addition of teamwork training to clinical training in simulated obstetric emergencies did not significantly impact perceptions of care related to communication. Teamwork training included a one-day course with lectures, video clips, and non-clinical activities emphasizing effective communication within multidisciplinary teams. Evidence suggested minimal differences in communication-related care perceptions across all scenarios when teamwork training was added. The review found no evidence on other maternal or fetal/neonatal outcomes related to this guideline question. Qualitative studies indicated that women, particularly first-time mothers, often feel apprehensive about labor and childbirth. They value the support and reassurance of healthcare professionals who are sensitive to their needs. Women also prefer receiving clear, relevant information from technically competent providers in an understandable manner. Effective communication is consistently appreciated as a key component of respectful maternity care (RMC). No research evidence was found on the cost or cost-effectiveness of communication interventions. However, such interventions are likely cost-effective if they improve maternity care quality, reduce medical interventions, and enhance birth outcomes. The primary cost associated with communication interventions is staff training, which may require lectures, workshops, and one-on-one sessions. Sustaining clinical training will also require resources for ongoing professional development. Cultural attitudes toward women and the low social status of women in some settings may also hinder implementation. Evidence suggests that without systemic changes, particularly in high-volume, resource-limited settings, communication interventions may not be feasible in the long term. Cultural attitudes toward marginalized women may further influence the success of these interventions. The WHO recommends that all women have a companion of their choice during labor and childbirth. This companion can be any person chosen by the woman to provide continuous support, such as a family member, friend, or trained labor support person (e.g., a doula). Evidence from a Cochrane review of 26 trials involving over 15,000 women showed that labor companionship reduces cesarean sections, instrumental vaginal births, and the use of pain relief. Midwife-led continuity-of-care models, where a known midwife or small group of midwives supports a woman throughout the antenatal, intrapartum, and postnatal periods, are recommended in settings with well-functioning midwifery programs. These models improve outcomes by fostering trust and continuity, though their implementation requires monitoring of resources, provider workload, and burnout. Policymakers in settings without robust midwifery programs should focus on scaling up the number and quality of midwives before implementing such models.
